newsitem.title: UK: Sheep cloning worries won't stop gene cure bid.
newsitem.headline: Sheep cloning worries won't stop gene cure bid.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

While the cloning of a sheep whipped up worries about mad scientists using genetic engineering to make copies of dictators like Stalin and Hitler, gene therapy companies are quietly working towards cures for AIDS, cystic fibrosis and cancer.
News that scientists in Scotland had cloned Dolly the sheep using an embryo cell and a cell from another sheep's mammary gland, sent shockwaves through the world's media.

But experts said companies like Therexsys, which may float on the stock market this year, and Oxford Biomedica which floated on the Alternative Investment Market in December are working on long-term gene based solutions to diseases.
Experts said that any public linking of the cloning development with worries over biotechnology and gene therapy was not justified.

"It's an absolutely incredible achievement, but it's not clear how this is related to gene therapy in humans. It might provide some useful model systems to investigate genetic disease, but that's still a long way away," said one analyst who declined to be named.

Scientists expressed excitement that this cloning breakthrough might lead to a myriad of new ways to help the human race. Herds of transgenic animals could be farmed for proteins, blood and organs. Gene therapy, with its ability to manipulate the core of human and animal life, could provide cures for killer diseases, and give hope to the crippled.

But the general public worried that all kinds of evil developments were also the logical extension of this breakthrough. Commentators said it would be possible for a woman to clone her own dead father. People with serious diseases could have themselves cloned for spare body parts.

U.S.President Bill Clinton, worried about the implications, asked an expert bioethics panel on Monday to review the legal and ethical ramifications of cloning with special regard to any implications for humans.
But worries that experiments with animals will quickly move on to humans are exagerrated, according to experts. Most western countries have strict rules against experimenting with humans.
Biotechnology, and its sister science gene therapy, has attracted much research funding in the United States and Britain.
Gene therapy was developed from biotechnology's ability to isolate and manipulate genes. Normal genes are introduced into defective or missing ones to correct disorders which are often hereditary.
There two types of gene therapy -- "germ-line" and "somatic". Cures seeking to use germ-line therapy would change inherited genes, and are against the law in most countries.
"Somatic gene therapy only affects the individual treated," said Paul Martin, researcher at Sussex Universitys Science Policy Research Unit.
"There are no ethical problems with this and there are various clinical trials underway in Britain, the U.S., and Europe targeting cancer, HIV/AIDS, and cystic fibrosis," Martin said.

"With cystic fibrosis, it's like conventional therapy in many ways. You spray a missing gene into the lungs of patients. It's just another form of drug delivery and is now seen as conventional," said Martin.
